title: When Children Seemingly Have Everything and Still Don’t Thrive
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Kevin Stinehart, an elementary teacher who runs his school's gardens, opens with a child who falls apart over a disputed move in a multiplication game. He argues that the child did not need a lecture on sportsmanship but practice at losing, disagreeing and recovering. His central claim is that many children are under-practiced rather than broken, because loved and well-resourced children can still lack one of nine developmental inputs, such as peer life, movement, independence or real responsibility. He uses the image of a plant that fails with almost everything it needs, and a sunflower rotting in Carolina clay, to show that growth depends on conditions being present together. He criticizes schools for answering struggle with more reminders, charts and adult control. He closes by calling for shared work among schools, neighborhoods, homes and civic groups to restore the conditions of a healthy childhood.
points: Behavior that looks like a motivation or attention problem is often a missing developmental input, so teachers should ask what practice the child has lacked before adding consequences.
Stinehart names nine inputs, including self-regulation, social connection, independence, and contribution, and says a child can have most of them and still fail to thrive.
Schools commonly respond to struggle with more adult management, such as reminders and behavior charts, which he argues cannot substitute for real play, movement, and responsibility.
Play is where many of the inputs overlap, so protecting recess and movement is a developmental matter rather than a reward.
Restoring childhood is framed as shared work across schools, neighborhoods, and homes rather than something individual parents can fix alone.
quotes: He did not need another adult lecture about sportsmanship. He did not need a laminated reminder about the value of talking it out when you get frustrated.

Practice losing without leaving. Practice disagreeing without collapsing. Practice feeling the heat of unfairness rise in his body, and discovering that the heat can pass without destroying the game, the friendship, or the afternoon.
A child can be loved and still lack real peer life. A child can be academically successful and still be starved for movement. A child can be safe and still be developmentally overmanaged.

I do not think children have become worse. I think many children are under-practiced in predictable places because the experiences that used to grow those capacities have been thinned out, managed away, or crowded off the calendar.
More adult management does not grow independence. More seat time does not replace movement. More lectures about perseverance do not replace real opportunities to persist through something hard.

We keep trying to fix children by adding more adult control to lives already crowded with adult control. We keep treating development like something we can install through programs, posters, and consequences.
